variant.text: All patient records originate from a de-identified hospital database collected during routine care between 2008 and 2019. The data are released under a credentialed-access data use agreement, and the source institution's review board determined that the study qualified for a waiver of consent.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.

To limit contamination, the test split is held out and distributed only through gated access, and we measured verbatim overlap between the test tasks and a public web corpus, finding no exact matches.

The agent cannot reach ground-truth answers at run time: the answer labels are stored in a separate evaluation service that has no network path from the agent sandbox, and they are not published in the repository.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
The grader checks both the intended state changes and that all other records remain unchanged, so out-of-scope modifications are detected and counted as failures.
A random-action agent succeeds on 3.1% of tasks, and the chance success rate for each metric is reported in the appendix.
A do-nothing agent that issues no actions scores 0.0% on all 120 tasks, and a random agent scores 2.5% on the same tasks.
All runs use temperature 0 and a fixed random seed, and each task is run three times; this repeated-run policy is described in the main text.
We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all model scores and test the difference between the two best models with a paired permutation test (p = 0.02).
Experiments were repeated multiple times.

We report 95% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping over tasks, so the resampling unit is the task; where several tasks share a patient, we resample patients instead to account for clustering.
Reliability measurement: each task executed eight times. We report pass^8 (share of tasks solved in all 8 runs) and agreement rates of the final environment state across these eight runs.

Tools are specified using JSON schemas with name, arguments, and types. Documentation for each tool declares whether it reads or modifies state and describes return values, including error messages for invalid arguments. Agent prompts include these tool descriptions.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.
The grader takes the final environment state as its input. We validated the grader on 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, finding a false-accept rate of 1% and a false-reject rate of 2%.

Web access is blocked during runs; retrieval is confined to the task environment, preventing answer leakage through search. A private held-out test split with concealed labels is excluded from all public surfaces. Released tasks include a canary string.
We report overall accuracy over all tasks.

The patient records are real de-identified records from a hospital database. Their use was approved under a data use agreement requiring credentialed access and de-identification by the safe harbour method, and the data are released under terms separate from the MIT code licence.
